brief:
Review explanation

Gradient descent on L(w) = w²/2: four learning rates, steps 0–8

interactive
Show gradient descent from w = 3 on L(w) = w²/2. Let me choose learning rates 0.2, 0.8, 1.2 and 2.1 and inspect steps 0 through 8. Show convergence, shrinking overshoots and divergence with all points visible.

Presentation
Static
Steps
Over time
Experiment

You'll see the curve L(w) = w²/2 with gradient descent points starting at w = 3. Each step is joined to the next by a line, so you can follow the path. A small side plot shows w against the step number, and labels give the current w, its loss and the update rule w ← (1 − η)w. Choose a learning rate of 0.2, 0.8, 1.2 or 2.1 and the path redraws: 0.2 slides slowly down to the minimum, 0.8 drops in almost at once, 1.2 jumps back and forth across zero with shorter jumps each time, and 2.1 jumps back and forth with longer jumps each time. This shows that each step multiplies w by (1 − η), so the path settles when that factor is between −1 and 1 and blows up when it isn't. Move the step slider from 0 to 8 to see the path build up one point at a time and read off the exact value at each step. The axes stay the same for every rate, so all points stay on screen, including the divergent path out to about w ≈ ±6.4.

ASSUMPTIONS 2
LIMITATIONS 2

findings.message: At η = 1.2, step 8, the points for steps 2–7 (|w| ≤ 0.12, i.e. ≤ ~5 px from w = 0) are hidden under the enlarged current-point circle (radius 14) at the bottom of the parabola. The shrinking overshoots can't be seen on the left plot, even though the request asks for all points to be visible. Shrinking the current-point marker or adding an inset or zoom near the minimum would fix this.
Near the minimum, the last few points on the parabola overlap each other and the enlarged current point, so they are hard to tell apart.
The warning sentence 'Overshoots, jumps grow: |-1.1| > 1, diverges' runs almost to the right edge of the card, with only a few pixels to spare. Moving it left or wrapping it would be safer.
